title: Captions on Presentation Videos: Why and How (blog explainer)

brief.story: A clear explainer of the post.

slides.title: Captions on Presentation Videos: Why and How
slides.notes: Turning lecture slides into video? Captions aren't an optional extra. They decide whether some of your audience can follow at all.

slides.title: Captions help far more viewers
slides.notes: Captions help far more people than you'd think. Learners in a second language, people on a train with the sound off, and anyone scanning back while revising.

slides.title: Burned-in or closed captions
bullets: Burned-in: part of the video image
Closed: separate SRT or VTT track
Viewers can turn closed captions off
slides.notes: Burned-in captions are always there, ideal for social feeds and email. Closed captions are a separate track viewers can switch off, often expected by an LMS.

slides.title: Write notes in short sentences
bullets: After: "It's worth forty per cent of your grade."
slides.notes: Captions are only as good as the words behind them. Break long sentences into short ones, write abbreviations out in full, and check names and jargon.

slides.title: Design slides with captions in mind
bullets: Keep the bottom of each slide clear
slides.notes: Captions sit near the bottom of the frame, so keep that area light. Use less text, strong contrast, and labels instead of colour alone.

slides.title: Ordinary slides in, captioned video out
slides.notes: Start with Basic to caption your deck, no subscription needed. On Pro, a.i. directs, timing animation and captions to your narration. Try it at powerpoint2vid.com.
